strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question: which latent factors multimodal contrastive learning can recover. Modeling shared information through noisy coupled variables is a useful direction.

The experiments cover synthetic recovery, CelebA traversals, four CLIP backbones, and several few-shot and distribution-shift settings. The synthetic results report strong recovery across multiple distributional mismatches.
Applying FastICA to frozen CLIP features is simple and accessible. The reported downstream improvements motivate further investigation of this inexpensive postprocessing approach.
weaknesses: The central proofs contain a fundamental error. Appendices A.4.1 and A.5.1 assert that optimality requires identical embeddings for every positive pair (Eqs. 27 and 49). The stated noisy conditional distributions have full support, so this requirement forces constant representations, already in the allowed case of independent nuisance variables. Collapse cannot simultaneously produce uniform representations. More concretely, in the spherical model with k > 0 and temperature 1/k, recovering the true latent variables gives normalized population loss -2I(zx;zt) < 0, whereas collapse gives 0. Thus the claimed necessary condition is false, undermining the proofs supporting the main identifiability claims.

The convex-body proof additionally assumes an incorrect marginal distribution. Uniform p(zx) and a normalized distance-based conditional do not generally yield uniform p(zt) on a bounded body at finite noise scale, because the conditional normalization varies near boundaries. Lemma 4.2 only concerns the limit as lambda approaches zero, but Eq. 56 uses uniformity as an exact equality without that restriction in Theorem 3.2. The permutation conclusion also requires the specific non-Euclidean metric restriction introduced in Appendix A.5.2, rather than an arbitrary norm-induced metric.

The theoretical justification for ICA disentanglement is insufficient even apart from the proof errors. Under the assumed uniform spherical distribution, every orthogonal rotation has the same distribution, so ICA cannot select a unique latent coordinate system. Having M-1 intrinsic degrees of freedom does not establish M-1 statistically independent Cartesian components. The proposed local-isometry/PCA argument for transferring the convex-body result to CLIP is also heuristic, without an approximation guarantee.

The downstream comparisons do not isolate the contribution of ICA. Appendix A.8 changes representation dimensionality to 300 components for ICA and 160 or 200 for PCA plus ICA, while lacking matched PCA-only and whitening-only baselines. An orthogonal ICA rotation within a fixed whitened subspace can be absorbed by an L2-regularized linear classifier without changing its objective. Consequently, the gains may arise from dimensionality reduction or whitening rather than disentanglement.

The CelebA evidence is qualitative and does not establish the claimed superiority in disentanglement. Counting 16 selected attributes versus counts reported in separate FactorVAE and beta-TCVAE studies is not a controlled comparison, particularly given CLIP's external pretraining. Some traversals explicitly combine attributes, such as 'Gender w/ Mustache.' Quantitative disentanglement measurements, component-selection criteria, and matched CLIP/PCA traversal baselines are needed.

The evaluation protocol and reproducibility need substantial clarification. Appendix A.8 says hyperparameters are selected using a validation split of each dataset; whether target-domain labels influence model selection must be clarified for the domain-generalization claims. The data used to fit PCA/ICA, synthetic training details, and variability across real-data runs are insufficiently documented. There is also a concrete reporting error: the four RN101 baseline target accuracies in Table 3 average to approximately 22.03, not 20.03, overstating the corresponding average improvement.
